quick.summary: Why removing names is never enough to protect customer privacy in small datasets.
quick.takeaway: Remove any combination of details that could point to one specific human.

beats.line: I shared the raw survey results. Someone recognized a specific customer.
Did I make a huge mistake doing that?
You did. Think of reading a private diary out loud.
Even without the name, the stories inside give it away.
I removed the names. I thought that was enough hiding.
It takes very little to expose personally identifiable information.
That is a mouthful. Can I just say personal direct details?
Good rule of thumb. Remove anything pointing to one human.
So I should group the ages and hide the exact titles.
Now you are protecting the people behind the numbers.

quiz.question: Which action best protects privacy when sharing survey data internally?
options: Grouping ages and replacing exact job titles with departments.
Deleting the first name column but leaving the last names.
Changing the font color of the identifying details to white.
Telling the team to keep the raw file a secret.
quiz.explanation: Grouping and generalizing data prevents colleagues from piecing together who submitted a specific response.

quiz.question: Removing a customer's name guarantees their data is fully anonymous.
quiz.explanation: A combination of other traits, like a specific job title and purchase history, can easily identify a person.
